on.question: Should we add rate protection before the next quarter?
on.reply: Yes—some rate protection is worth considering: the company’s rate mismatch (duration gap) is negative 3.59 years, and a 1 bp fall in rates reduces surplus by $26.9 million. Each additional 10% of rate hedging costs $0.004 billion per quarter. The hedge would cushion falling rates, but it would cost money and give up some benefit if rates rise; the inflation wire is only a hint, not a forecast. I would not treat this as a case for a full hedge based on the information available.

on.question: What happens to us if one of our derivatives dealers fails?
on.reply: Our current record shows no rate or equity hedges, one dealer, and no collateral posted, so there is no listed hedge position whose value we could lose if that dealer failed. If we add hedges, a dealer failure could leave us without money the bank owes and require us to pay the replacement cost to set the hedge up elsewhere. Collateral can limit that loss, while using more than one dealer reduces our reliance on a single bank; both come with added costs. I do not have a figure for the potential replacement cost.

off.question: What is our biggest risk right now?
off.reply: Our biggest risk is the rate mismatch (duration gap): it is negative 3.59 years, so falling rates reduce surplus. A 1 bp fall in rates would cut surplus by $26.9 million. Liquidity is also tight: the liquidity ratio is 101.7%, just above its 100% floor, while the capital ratio is 159.6% and green. In short, rate exposure is the main concern; liquidity has little room for stress.

off.question: How much would our surplus change if interest rates fell by 1%?

facts.name: surplus change for a 1% fall ($bn, from net DV01)

off.reply: If interest rates fell by 1%, our surplus would decrease by about $2.69 billion on today’s book, assuming other market conditions stayed unchanged. This is a hypothetical stress-test result, not a forecast of what will happen this quarter.

off.question: What is our capital ratio, and how close are we to the floor?
off.reply: Our capital ratio is 159.6%, compared with the 100% floor. We are above the floor, and the dashboard marks capital green.

off.question: Should we hedge more of the stock-market guarantees?
off.reply: More protection is a reasonable option, but the figures do not make it an automatic yes. The company currently has no equity puts; a hypothetical stock fall of 10% would cost the guarantees $0.71 billion gross, while the whole-company stress test shows a $0.79 billion surplus decline. Those figures describe different things, so do not add them together. Each extra 10% of put hedging costs $0.0085 billion per quarter, whether or not markets fall; it would reduce some guarantee risk but add ongoing cost. The news signal is not a forecast, so this is a trade-off, not a prediction.

off.question: Should we sell some junk and BBB bonds and buy government bonds?
off.reply: A selective shift could make sense: government bonds have a much lower capital charge than investment-grade corporate bonds or below-investment-grade bonds, and they remove credit-spread and default exposure on the amount moved. But you would give up yield: the current yields are 3.31% for government bonds, 4.09% for investment-grade corporates, and 5.65% for below-investment-grade bonds. A move into longer-duration government bonds may also help narrow our negative rate mismatch, though the effect depends on how much you move. The scale matters: if all credit spreads widened by 100 bp, the portfolio bond loss is $4.1 billion, but the estimated surplus loss after liability offsets is $0.22 billion; I would assess the size of any shift rather than sell broadly just because the bonds are riskier.

off.question: Do we have enough cash on hand if policyholders start surrendering?
off.reply: For the modeled rate-rise and higher-surrender scenario, the extra surrender outflow is $1.07 billion, and our $5.7 billion of cash alone covers it. Looking at the broader 90-day stress, cash and government bonds after stressed sale discounts total $8.69 billion against $8.54 billion of possible outflows: the liquidity ratio is 101.7%, just above the 100% floor. So we appear able to meet the modeled need, but the cushion is thin; if those liquid assets ran out, we would have to sell other investments at larger discounts.

off.question: What would a 10% fall in the stock market do to us?
off.reply: A 10% stock-market fall on today’s book would reduce our surplus—the cushion after what we own is set against what we owe—by $0.79bn. In this hypothetical, the change comes entirely from equity exposure; the other modeled causes show no change. This is a what-if, not a forecast of this quarter.

off.question: What would it cost per quarter to close half of our rate mismatch with swaps?
off.reply: Setting the rate hedge to 50%—half of the current mismatch—would cost $0.0202 billion per quarter. The preview shows the rate mismatch (duration gap) narrowing from -3.59 years to -1.8 years; the hedge reduces the exposure but does not eliminate it.

off.question: Should we add rate protection before the next quarter?
off.reply: Some added rate protection is worth considering: our rate mismatch (duration gap) is negative 3.59 years, and a 1 bp fall in rates reduces surplus by $26.9 million. Each extra 10% of rate hedging costs $0.004 billion per quarter, so more protection trades lower exposure to falling rates for ongoing cost and less benefit if rates rise. Capital is above its floor, while liquidity is only just above its floor; the news wire is a hint, not a forecast, so I would not size a hedge as a bet on rates moving one way.

off.question: What happens to us if one of our derivatives dealers fails?
off.reply: Right now, we have no rate or equity hedges, and the dashboard shows no uncollateralized dealer exposure, so a dealer failure has no current hedge value shown as at risk. If we add derivatives later, a failed dealer might not pay what it owes us, and replacing the hedge could cost more; that is counterparty risk. Collateral can limit the unpaid amount, while using more dealers can reduce reliance on one bank, but both protections have costs. Neither protection is free—risk has a remarkably good sense of timing.
